rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طلحة
rows.claim: Ali ibn Abi Talha's transmitted Medinan list includes al-Fajr, along with al-Layl and other sūras.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طلحة قال نزلت بالمدينة سورة البقرة وآل عمران

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada's Medinan list omits al-Fajr and says the rest of the Qur'an was revealed in Mecca, implying al-Fajr is Meccan in this account.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة قال نزل في المدينة من القرآن البقرة وآل عمران والنساء

rows.speaker: ابن الحصار
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hassar classifies twenty sūras as Medinan by agreement, twelve as disputed, and all remaining sūras as Meccan by agreement.
rows.anchor: المدني باتفاق عشرون سورة والمختلف فيه اثنتا عشرة سورة وما عدا ذلك مكي باتفاق

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: Ali ibn al-Husayn says Iqra was the first Meccan revelation, with al-Muʾminun or al-ʿAnkabut last; al-Mutaffifin began the Medinan revelations, Baraʾa ended them, and al-Najm was the first sūra publicly recited at Mecca.
rows.anchor: قال سمعت علي بن الحسين يقول أول سورة نزلت بمكة ﴿ اقرأ باسم ربك ﴾ وآخر سورة نزلت بها المؤمنون

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar reports agreement that al-Baqara was the first sūra revealed in Medina.
rows.anchor: وفي شرح البخاري لابن حجر اتفقوا على أن سورة البقرة أول سورة أنزلت بالمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti questions the claimed agreement about al-Baqara because of the preceding report from Ali ibn al-Husayn.
rows.anchor: وفي دعوى الاتفاق نظر لقول علي بن الحسين المذكور

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi is cited for the view that al-Qadr was the first sūra revealed in Medina.
rows.anchor: عن الواقدي إن أول سورة نزلت بالمدينة سورة القدر

rows.speaker: جابر بن زيد
rows.claim: Jabir ibn Zayd's reported Meccan revelation order places al-Fajr tenth and al-ʿAsr thirteenth.
rows.anchor: عن جابر بن زيد قال أول ما أنزل الله من القرآن بمكة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: The reported order of Ibn Masʿud's codex places al-Fajr and al-ʿAsr among the mufassal sūras, with al-Fajr preceding al-ʿAsr.
rows.anchor: تأليف مصحف عبد الله بن مسعود الطوال البقرة والنساء وآل عمران

rows.speaker: الموصلي
rows.claim: Al-Mawsili says “then he looked” is the Qur'an's shortest verse; ʿAmma, al-Fajr, and al-Duha are equally short.
rows.anchor: قال الموصلي وعدوا قوله ﴿ ثم نظر ﴾ آية وليس في القرآن أقصر منها أما مثلها فعم والفجر والضحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “al-Fajr wa-layālin,” the tanwīn on the defective broken plural is compensatory for a final omitted weak letter.
rows.anchor: وتنوين العوض إما عن حرف آخر مفاعل المعتل نحو ﴿ والفجر وليال ﴾

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One classification puts al-Fajr among sūras containing neither abrogating nor abrogated material, while placing al-ʿAsr among sūras containing both.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم سور القرآن باعتبار الناسخ والمنسوخ أقسام قسم ليس فيه ناسخ ولا منسوخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says this four-part classification of sūras according to abrogation is open to question, as later discussion shows.
rows.anchor: كذا قال وفيه نظر يعرف مما سيأتي

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki distinguishes an obligation abrogated by another obligation when the former can no longer be practiced, exemplified by confinement of adulteresses replaced by the penalty.
rows.anchor: قال مكي الناسخ أقسام فرض نسخ فرضا ولا يجوز العمل بالأول

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki also identifies an obligation replaced by another obligation while the earlier obligation may still be practiced, as with the verse of steadfastness.
rows.anchor: وفرض نسخ فرضا ويجوز العمل بالأول كآية المصابرة

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki's third case is a recommended act later made obligatory, such as fighting first being recommended and then required.
rows.anchor: وفرض نسخ ندبا كالقتال كان ندبا ثم صار فرضا

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki's fourth case is a recommended act replacing an obligation: night vigil was replaced by reciting what is easy of the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وندب نسخ فرضا كقيام الليل نسخ بالقراءة في قوله ﴿ فاقرؤوا ما تيسر من القرآن ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti divides Qur'anic abrogation into three kinds and begins with cases where both the recitation and ruling are abrogated.
rows.anchor: النسخ في القرآن على ثلاثة أضرب أحدها ما نسخ تلاوته وحكمه معا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that ten known instances of nursing were revealed, then replaced by five; she said the wording was still being recited at the Prophet's death, and the report is in both Ṣaḥīḥs.
rows.anchor: قالت عائشة كان فيما أنزل ( عشر رضعات معلومات فنسخن بخمس معلومات فتوفي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهن مما يقرأ من القرآن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti notes the apparent implication that the nursing wording remained recited and explains that its recitation was either abrogated near the Prophet's death or not known to everyone until after his death.
rows.anchor: وقد تكلموا في قولها ( وهن مما يقرأ ) فإن ظاهره بقاء التلاوة وليس كذلك

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abu Musa al-Ashʿari says the nursing passage was revealed and then withdrawn.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو موسى الأشعري نزلت ثم رفعت

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki says the nursing example is unusual because neither the abrogated text nor its abrogator is recited, and he knows no parallel.
rows.anchor: وقال مكي هذا المثال فيه المنسوخ غير متلو والناسخ أيضا غير متلو ولا أعلم له نظيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind removes a ruling while leaving its recitation; despite extensive lists, this kind is truly rare, as Ibn al-ʿArabi carefully showed.
rows.anchor: الضرب الثاني ما نسخ حكمه دون تلاوته وهذا الضرب هو الذي فيه الكتب المؤلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says all sūras begin in one of ten forms of speech; the oath is the fifth form and opens fifteen sūras.
rows.anchor: افتتح سور القرآن بعشرة أنواع من الكلام لا يخرج شيء من السور عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by al-Fajr refers to the beginning of the day.
rows.anchor: الفجر بمبدأ النهار والشمس بآية النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by al-ʿAsr refers either to the day's latter part or to time as a whole.
rows.anchor: العصر بالشطر الآخر أو بجملة الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One oath pattern proceeds to an assertion of God's oneness, as in the oath by those arrayed in ranks.
rows.anchor: فالأول كقوله ﴿ والصافات صفا ﴾ إلى قوله ﴿ إن إلهكم لواحد ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second pattern explicitly calls attention to the oath's greatness before asserting that the Qur'an is noble.
rows.anchor: والثاني كقوله ﴿ فلا أقسم بمواقع النجوم وإنه لقسم لو تعلمون عظيم إنه لقرآن كريم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third pattern follows the oath with a declaration, as in the assertion that Muhammad is among the messengers and the assertion that his companion did not err.
rows.anchor: والثالث كقوله ﴿ يس والقرآن الحكيم إنك لمن المرسلين ﴾ ﴿ والنجم إذا هوى ما ضل صاحبكم وما غوى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth pattern uses a sequence of oaths to affirm that the promised event and judgment are real.
rows.anchor: والرابع كقوله ﴿ والذاريات ﴾ إلى قوله ﴿ إنما توعدون لصادق وإن الدين لواقع ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth pattern pairs an oath with a proposition about human action or condition; al-ʿAsr exemplifies it by declaring humanity in loss.
rows.anchor: والعصر إن الإنسان لفي خسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to an oath is often omitted when the object sworn by already indicates the assertion; that omission is more forceful and concise.
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما يحذف الجواب إذا كان في نفس المقسم به دلالة على المقسم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fajr passage invokes times containing the great rites of pilgrimage and humble worship of God; their significance implies the honor of what Muhammad and Abraham brought.
rows.anchor: والفجر ﴾ الآيات فإنها أزمان تتضمن أفعالا معظمة من المناسك وشعائر الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by forenoon and night testifies to God's favor on and honor of the Prophet, thereby affirming his prophethood and the resurrection and recompense.
rows.anchor: ومن لطائف القسم قوله ﴿ والضحى والليل إذا سجى ﴾ الآيات أقسم تعالى على إنعامه على رسوله وإكرامه له

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani says exegetes regard the testimony verse as among the Qur'an's most difficult passages in ruling, meaning, and syntax.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني ذكر المفسرون أن قوله تعالى ﴿ يا أيها الذين آمنوا شهادة بينكم ﴾ الآية

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another scholar says the verse about adornment gathers the foundations of the law: command, prohibition, permissibility, and report.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره قوله تعالى ﴿ يا بني آدم خذوا زينتكم ﴾ الآية جمعت أصول أحكام الشريعة

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani explains the “best of stories” as Joseph's story, which gathers many opposites and human situations beyond the capacity of people to describe fully.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني في العجائب في قوله تعالى ﴿ نحن نقص عليك أحسن القصص ﴾ قيل هو قصة يوسف

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda reports Ruʾba's judgment that “proclaim what you are commanded” is the Qur'an's most eloquent expression in Arabic.
rows.anchor: ذكر أبو عبيدة عن رؤبة ما في القرآن أعرب من قوله ﴿ فاصدع بما تؤمر ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh says this is the Qur'an's only expression displaying all three dialect forms of negative mā: the majority read it accusatively, some nominatively, and Ibn Masʿud adds bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن خالويه في كتاب ليس ليس في كلام العرب لفظ جمع لغات ما النافية إلا حرف واحد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “yathanūni ṣudūrahum” is the Qur'an's sole form on the pattern afʿawʿal.
rows.anchor: وليس في القرآن لفظ على ( افعوعل ) إلا في قراءة ابن عباس / ألا إنهم يثنوني صدورهم /

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An unnamed authority calls al-Baqara the longest sūra, al-Kawthar the shortest, the debt verse the longest āya, al-Duha and al-Fajr the shortest, and “fa-asqaynākumūhu” the longest written word.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم أطول سورة في القرآن البقرة وأقصرها الكوثر وأطول آية فيه آية الدين

words: ثم أنزل عليكم من بعد الغم أمنة
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source notes two verses, in al-ʿImran and al-Fath, each containing every letter of the alphabet.
rows.anchor: وفي القرآن آيتان جمعت كل منهما حروف المعجم ﴿ ثم أنزل عليكم من بعد الغم أمنة ﴾ الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only two places have ḥāʾ immediately followed by ḥāʾ without an intervening letter: these phrases from al-Baqara and al-Kahf.
rows.anchor: وليس فيه حاء بعد حاء بلا حاجز إلا في موضعين ﴿ عقدة النكاح حتى ﴾ ﴿ لا أبرح حتى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The only adjacent kāf-kāf sequences without an intervening letter occur in “manāsikakum” and “mā salakakum.”
rows.anchor: ولا كافان كذلك إلا ﴿ مناسككم ﴾ ﴿ ما سلككم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “whoever seeks a religion other than Islam” is the only place with two ghayn letters adjacent without an intervening letter.
rows.anchor: ولا غينان كذلك إلا ﴿ ومن يبتغ غير الإسلام ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The debt verse is the Qur'an's only āya containing twenty-three kāf letters.
rows.anchor: ولا آية فيها ثلاثة وعشرون كافا إلا آية الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two inheritance verses are the only āyāt each containing thirteen instances of the waqf mark.
rows.anchor: ولا آيتان فيهما ثلاثة عشر وقفا إلا آيتا المواريث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In its added-letter inventory, the source lists the written form “jāy” in al-Zumar and al-Fajr, and notes that “ibn” is written with hamza throughout.
rows.anchor: وبين الياء والجيم في ( جاي ) في الزمر والفجر وكتبت ( ابن ) بالهمزة مطلقا

rows.speaker: المراكشي
rows.claim: Al-Marrakushi says added letters in forms such as “jāyʾ” and “nabāʾ” convey awe, grandeur, threat, and warning; the extra letters in “bi-aydin” magnify God's power.
rows.anchor: قال المراكشي وإنما زيدت هذه الأحرف في هذه الكلمات نحو ( جايء ) و ( نبائ ) ونحوهما للتهويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source catalogs added alifs after waw in plural nouns and in certain verb forms, with listed exceptions.
rows.anchor: زيدت ألف بعد الواو آخر اسم مجموع نحو ( بنوا إسرائيل ) ( ملاقوا ربهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also lists added alifs after hamza written as waw and in several specific forms, including “miʾa,” “miʾatayn,” and definite nouns ending in alif.
rows.anchor: وبعد الهمزة المرسومة واوا نحو ( تفتؤا ) وفي مائة ومائتين والظنونا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orthography adds yāʾ in several listed forms, including “nabāʾ al-mursalīn,” “malāʾihi,” and “bi-ayydikum.”
rows.anchor: وزيدت ياء في ( نبائ المرسلين ) و ( ملإيه ) ( ملإيهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extra wāw is written in “ulū” and its derivatives, and in “sa-urīkum.”
rows.anchor: وزيدت واو في ( أولوا ) وفروعه و ( سأوريكم )

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani explains some extra letters as remnants of an older script in which alif, wāw, and yāʾ represented the short vowels fatḥa, ḍamma, and kasra.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني في العجائب كانت صورة الفتحة في الخطوط قبل الخط العربي ألفا

rows.speaker: ابن حبيب
rows.claim: Ibn Habib says most of the Qur'an was revealed during daytime, while examples of night revelation were separately collected.
rows.anchor: قال ابن حبيب نزل أكثر القرآن نهارا وأما الليل فتتبعت له أمثلة

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: In the Ṣaḥīḥayn report from Ibn ʿUmar, people at Quba were told at dawn that the Prophet had received revelation the previous night ordering them to face the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: من حديث ابن عمر بينما الناس بقباء في صلاة الصبح إذا أتاهم آت فقال إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قد أنزل عليه الليلة قرآن

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Muslim's report from Anas says the qibla verse came while the Prophet prayed toward Jerusalem; Banu Salima were told during the dawn prayer and turned toward the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: وروى مسلم عن أنس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يصلي ببيت المقدس فنزلت ﴿ قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء ﴾

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Baraʾ's Ṣaḥīḥayn report says the qibla change came after sixteen or seventeen months; the first prayer toward the Kaʿba was ʿAsr, supporting a daytime revelation between noon and ʿAsr.
rows.anchor: عن البراء أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم صلى قبل بيت المقدس ستة عشر أو سبعة عشر شهرا

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: جلال الدين
rows.claim: Qadi Jalal al-Din judges nighttime revelation stronger, since Quba learned at dawn and it seems unlikely the Prophet delayed conveying the command from the prior afternoon.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي جلال الدين والأرجح بمقتضى الاستدلال نزولها بالليل لأن قضية أهل قباء كانت في الصبح

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar prefers daytime revelation: the news reached people inside Medina at ʿAsr and Quba at dawn; “last night” can refer idiomatically to part of the previous day and the following night.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حجر الأقوى أن نزولها كان نهارا والجواب عن حديث ابن عمر

words: قد نرى تقلب وجهك في السماء
rows.speaker: أبو سعيد بن المعلى
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti cites al-Nasaʾi's report from Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla: the Prophet recited the qibla verse from the minbar, then descended and prayed noon, supporting daytime revelation.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد بن المعلى قال مررنا يوما ورسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قاعد على المنبر

rows.speaker: الجعبري
rows.claim: Al-Jaʿbari defines an āya as Qur'an composed of sentences, explicitly or implicitly, with a beginning or ending within a sūra; its name signifies a mark.
rows.anchor: قال الجعبري حد الآية قرآن مركب من جمل ولو تقديرا ذو مبدإ أو مقطع

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another definition calls an āya a portion of the Qur'an separated from what precedes and follows it.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره الآية طائفة من القرآن منقطعة عما قبلها وما بعدها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation calls each counted unit an āya because it proves the messenger's truth and the challengers' inability.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي الواحدة من المعدودات في السور سميت به لأنها علامة على صدق من أتى بها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further explanation derives the name from the āya marking the break between its surrounding speech.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنها علامة على علامة إنقطاع ما قبلها من الكلام وانقطاعه مما بعدها

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi and some colleagues say that definition could label less than a full āya an āya, except that revelation fixed the divisions as they now stand.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي وبعض أصحابنا يجوز على هذا القول تسمية أقل من الآية آية

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr al-Dani says the only word that forms an āya by itself is “mudhāmmatān.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو الداني لا أعلم كلمة هي وحدها آية إلا قوله ﴿ مدهامتان ﴾

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Other scholars add “wa-l-najm,” “wa-l-duha,” and “wa-l-ʿasr” as standalone āyāt, along with sūra openings for those who count them so.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره بل فيه غيرها مثل ﴿ والنجم ﴾ ﴿ والضحى ﴾ ﴿ والعصر ﴾

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the correct basis for āya boundaries is prophetic specification: each unit's separation from neighboring speech is known by transmitted instruction, not analogy.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم الصحيح أن الآية إنما تعلم بتوقيف من الشارع كمعرفة السورة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari likewise says verse counts are transmitted and cannot be inferred by analogy, explaining why some disjointed-letter openings count as āyāt and others do not.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري الآيات علم توقيفي لا مجال للقياس فيه ولذلك عدوا ﴿ الم ﴾ آية

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti cites Ahmad's report from Ibn Masʿud that the Prophet recited one of the Hā-Mīm sūras, identified as al-Ahqaf, and used the report's “thirty” designation as evidence about verse counting.
rows.anchor: عن زر عن ابن مسعود قال أقرأني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم سورة من الثلاثين من آل حم

rows.speaker: الموصلي
rows.claim: Al-Mawsili divides sūras into three groups: counts with no disagreement, counts differing in detail only, and counts differing both in total and detail; his lists include forty, four, and seventy sūras respectively.
rows.anchor: قال الموصلي ثم سور القرآن على ثلاثة أقسام قسم لم يختلف فيه لا في إجمال ولا في تفصيل

rows.speaker: المدني الأخير والباقون
rows.claim: Al-ʿAsr has three verses: the later Medinan count treats “wa-tawāṣaw bi-l-ḥaqq” as a verse but not “wa-l-ʿaṣr”; the other counters do the reverse.
rows.anchor: العصر ثلاث عد المدني الأخير ﴿ وتواصوا بالحق ﴾ دون ﴿ والعصر ﴾ وعكس الباقون

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority count al-Fatiha as seven verses, with Kufan and Meccan counters counting the basmala but not “anʿamta ʿalayhim,” and others doing the reverse.
rows.anchor: الفاتحة الجمهور سبع فعد الكوفي والمكي البسملة دون أنعمت عليهم وعكس الباقون

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan counts al-Fatiha as eight verses by including both the basmala and “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن ثمان فعدهما وبعضهم ست فلم يعدهما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some count al-Fatiha as six verses by counting neither the basmala nor “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
rows.anchor: وبعضهم ست فلم يعدهما وآخر تسع فعدهما و ﴿ إياك نعبد ﴾

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another view counts al-Fatiha as nine verses, including both the basmala and “iyyāka naʿbud.”
rows.anchor: وآخر تسع فعدهما و ﴿ إياك نعبد ﴾

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha verse by verse, counted the basmala as a verse, and did not count “ʿalayhim”; al-Suyuti says this supports the majority's seven-verse count.
rows.anchor: عن أم سلمة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقرأ
